claims.text: High-entropy nanoalloys exhibit high-temperature structural and chemical stability.
High mixing entropy intrinsically suppresses bulk lattice diffusion in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Intrinsic suppression of bulk lattice diffusion is the primary cause of high-temperature stability rather than grain-boundary surface segregation.
Sputtering can produce nanocrystalline high-entropy alloy films having a uniform single-phase structure and high grain-boundary density.
Systematically changing grain size changes the grain-boundary amount and surface-to-volume ratio.
The proposed controlled atmosphere prevents extrinsic oxidation or corrosion during high-temperature exposure.
Grain boundaries provide increased interfacial area for chemical segregation.
Suppression of atomic mobility in the alloy lattice stabilizes the structure at elevated temperatures.
If intrinsic lattice-diffusion suppression dominates, changing grain size should not significantly change phase or chemical stability.
If surface segregation governs stability, fine-grained samples should exhibit more phase degradation and chemical inhomogeneity than coarse-grained samples.
After high-temperature exposure, samples with different grain sizes are predicted to retain similar phase integrity and chemical homogeneity.
A coarse-grained version of the same alloy has minimal grain-boundary effects relative to the nanocrystalline samples.
The prediction is restricted to conditions under which the alloy remains single phase, processing-induced composition variations are minimal, and environmental oxidation or corrosion is controlled.
Significantly greater degradation, chemical inhomogeneity, or diffusion rates in fine-grained samples than in the coarse-grained baseline would falsify the proposed primary mechanism.
